title: A/B Price Testing: Guide for Ecommerce Businesses
summary: Learn about the different elements you can run A/B price tests on, and how to conduct an A/B test to land on an ideal price and presentation.
body_markdown:
A/B price testing can help you make data-backed pricing decisions by showing how customers respond to different prices, discounts, and offers. It allows you to use actual purchasing behavior to inform your pricing strategy.


Choosing the right price for your products can have a significant impact on whether customers buy. In a[2025 Ipsos survey](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/getting-value-their-money-key-online-shoppers-3) , 68% of online shoppers said price was a key factor when buying products online, and the same percentage said they always or often compare prices when shopping online.


This guide covers different pricing elements you can test and offers steps for designing, running, and evaluating A/B pricing tests.


## What is A/B price testing?


[A/B testing](https://www.shopify.com/blog/the-complete-guide-to-ab-testing) , also known as[split testing](https://www.shopify.com/blog/split-testing-pricing) , lets you present two different pricing options to two sets of customers to see which resonates best. You split your audience into two groups—a control group (A) and a test group (B). Over a set time period, the control group continues to see the existing pricing, while the test group sees the pricing variation. You then gather and analyze data on how they respond to help determine your optimal pricing going forward.


This testing method lets you evaluate various pricing models or other price differences with a subset of customers before you implement them more widely. For example, you can compare different price points, discount presentations,[product bundles](https://www.shopify.com/blog/bundling-for-retail) , or other pricing strategies to see which performs better on metrics such as[conversion rate](https://www.shopify.com/blog/ecommerce-conversion-rate) , revenue, or[average order value (AOV)](https://www.shopify.com/blog/average-order-value) .


While many factors such as production costs and competitor pricing can help you set product pricing, A/B price testing adds information about customer behavior—how customers actually respond to your pricing. The results of these pricing experiments can provide insight into customers’ price sensitivity and how they perceive the value of your products.


A/B price testing is different from dynamic pricing. A dynamic pricing strategy involves altering prices in real time based on customer demand. It's commonly used for products and services with high price elasticity, like airline tickets, hotels, and ride shares. By contrast, A/B price testing involves running tests to find an ideal price or presentation for your products.


### When is A/B price testing useful?


A/B price testing methods are most useful when you have a specific pricing question to answer and enough traffic, sales, and inventory to generate meaningful results. It can be less useful for low-volume products or during periods when promotions, seasonal demand, or other changes could make it difficult to determine whether pricing caused the results.


Price testing also comes with legal and ethical considerations, particularly when businesses use customer data to determine who receives an offer. Testing different prices can also create customer trust issues if shoppers discover that other customers were offered a lower price.


## Types of A/B price testing


- Base price
- Compare-at price and discount presentation
- Bundle pricing
- Quantity discounts
- Free shipping thresholds


A/B price testing can involve much more than testing two different retail prices for the same product. You can experiment with how you present discounts, set free shipping thresholds, and more.


Here are a few pricing components you can test:


### Base price


One way to A/B test is to see how customers respond to your product’s base price. For example, say you sell handmade wool socks and related accessories online. You could offer the same pair of socks to one group for $15 and the other group for a higher price of $20, and then compare the buying behavior of each group to land on a final, ideal price.


### Compare-at price and discount presentation


When you lower the price of an item, you can visually display the savings by presenting the compare-at price (the original price) and the sales price. You can test how customers perceive the value of a discount by showing two groups different discount presentations for the same-priced item. For example, if you discount your $15 wool socks to $12, you could show one group “$3 off” and the other “20% off” and compare their responses.


Shopify lets you[add a badge](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/products/details/product-pricing/sale-pricing) with a sale message to your product listing and collection pages, and also lets you customize sale price styling.


### Bundle pricing


Offering customers a discount when they buy a curated set of items in a single order can increase the perceived value of your products. For example, you could offer your $15 wool socks individually or bundle them with a $25 wool beanie for $35. In an A/B test, you could compare how customers respond when offered the socks alone versus the discounted bundle, or show customers two different bundles to see which one generates more sales.


### Quantity discounts


An example of the “buy more, save more” sales strategy, quantity discounts offer a progressive discount when a customer buys multiples of the same product. For example, you could offer one pair of wool socks for $15, three for $40, or six for $70. Your A/B test could compare a single-priced item against the quantity discount to see if customers buy more pairs for a cheaper price.


### Free shipping thresholds


Test different minimum order values for[free shipping](https://www.shopify.com/blog/free-shipping-and-conversion) on your control group and your test group to see how they affect average order value. For example, you could offer one group free shipping on orders of $50 or more and the other free shipping on orders of $60 or more.


## How to run an A/B price test


1. Define your test goal and key metrics
2. Develop your hypothesis
3. Randomize and assign your audience
4. Design and run your test
5. Analyze the results—and keep testing


A well-designed A/B price test isolates one pricing variable so you can determine whether it affected customer behavior. That requires setting a clear goal, randomly assigning customers to test groups, and collecting enough data to draw meaningful conclusions.


Follow these steps to design and[run your A/B test](https://www.shopify.com/blog/ab-testing) :


### 1. Define your test goal and key metrics


Start with the big picture: What do you want to improve, and how will you measure success? Your goal should be measurable, such as increasing revenue, improving conversion rates, or raising AOV.


Choose a key metric that directly reflects that goal. Keep in mind that improving one metric doesn’t necessarily mean the pricing change is better for your business overall. For example, lowering a product’s price might increase its conversion rate while reducing the revenue or profit generated by each sale.


### 2. Develop your hypothesis


Decide which pricing decision might affect the goal and key metric you identified, and then choose a product to which you’ll apply this pricing decision. To increase your chances of collecting enough data to achieve[statistical significance](https://www.shopify.com/blog/statistical-significance) , focus on a high-volume product that gets significant traffic.


Once you’ve got a pricing decision and product in mind, create your hypothesis. A hypothesis describes the expected result of your A/B test in clear, specific, and testable language. Hypotheses follow a general structure: “If we do X (your proposed pricing decision on your proposed product), Y (your desired result) will increase/decrease.” For example, “If we offer a discounted bundle of wool socks and a beanie, AOV will increase by 15%.”


Make sure you focus on only one variable of your pricing plans. If you test multiple variables at once, you won’t be able to tell which one is making an impact.


### 3. Randomize and assign your audience


Randomly assign which target customers will see your experimental pricing offer rather than choosing them based on specific characteristics. In a 50/50 A/B test, half of your customers continue to see existing pricing, while the other half sees the offer you’re testing. Random assignment helps ensure that differences between the two test groups don’t skew your results.


Select eligible Shopify stores in the US have early access to Shopify’s[Smart Pricing app](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/products/details/product-pricing/smart-pricing/create-experiment) , which splits your catalog into control and experimental versions and randomly assigns 50% of traffic to each.


Some A/B pricing tests may only be relevant to certain customers.[Customer segmentation](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-customer-segmentation) —dividing your customers into groups based on shared characteristics or behaviors—can ensure you’re reaching only those shoppers. For example, if you want to see how existing customers respond to a new pricing offer, you could limit the experiment only to that customer segment and randomly assign half of them to see your usual pricing and half to see the experimental pricing.


### 4. Design and run your test


Use an[A/B testing tool](https://www.shopify.com/blog/ab-testing-tools) to create and display the pricing variation you want to test. For example,[Intelligems](https://www.intelligems.io/) lets you test[product prices](https://www.shopify.com/blog/how-to-price-your-product) , discounts, bundles, quantity discounts, and free shipping thresholds.[Shoplift](https://www.shoplift.ai/) and Smart Pricing from Shopify also offer product price testing.


Before launching your test, consider factors that could affect the reliability of your results:


-


Make sure you have enough traffic and sales to produce meaningful results. A/B testing tools may help determine whether you have sufficient data and whether your results are statistically significant.


-


Make sure your test product has ample inventory. If it sells out during the experiment, your test results could be affected.


-


Run the test long enough to draw a reliable conclusion. For example, Shopify Smart Pricing indicates when results have reached statistical significance at 95% confidence.


-


Avoid periods with unusual shopping behavior, such as major holidays, unless those periods are relevant to what you’re testing.


-


Be aware of external factors, such as a competitor changing its pricing or running a sale, that could affect customer behavior during your test.


### 5. Analyze the results—and keep testing


After you run your test, analyze your results against the goal and key metric you established in the first step. If the results support your hypothesis and are statistically significant, you can implement the pricing change. If your test didn’t give you the results you expected, you’ve still gained valuable customer information—and there are plenty of other pricing components you can test.


Just don’t test everything at once: Continue to approach A/B testing systematically, one hypothesis at a time.

## Is A/B price testing legal?


A/B price testing is generally permitted, but businesses need to comply with applicable consumer protection, privacy, anti-discrimination, and pricing laws. Requirements vary depending on where you operate and how you conduct your test.


In the US, federal and state laws may apply depending on how a pricing test is conducted. Businesses should avoid pricing practices that unlawfully discriminate against customers or use customer data in ways that violate federal or state law.


Some states have adopted more specific requirements. For example,[New York requires](https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2025/attorney-general-james-warns-new-yorkers-about-algorithmic-pricing-new-law-takes) businesses to disclose when they use consumers’ personal data to set individualized prices.


Random A/B price testing is different from personalized pricing based on information about an individual. However, the distinction can become less clear when businesses use customer data to create different customer segments for a test. Businesses that use customer data to determine who receives a pricing offer should pay particular attention to disclosure requirements. In a proposed 2026 enforcement policy statement, the[Federal Trade Commission (FTC) warned](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/p034101-ftc-enforcement-policy-statement-re-personalized-pricing-proposed-for-public-comment.pdf) that using personal data to personalize prices without adequate disclosure may violate federal consumer protection law.


In the EU, personalized pricing based on automated decision-making is permitted in principle, but businesses must inform consumers when a price has been personalized this way. EU rules also restrict price discrimination based on a customer’s nationality or country of residence.


Even when a pricing experiment is legal, consider how customers might perceive it. Customers who discover that someone else was offered a lower price for the same product may view that practice as unfair. Testing how you present value—such as compare-at pricing, discounts, bundles, and quantity discounts—can let you experiment with pricing without necessarily showing different customers different base prices.


## A/B price testing FAQ


### What is A/B price testing?


A/B price testing lets you compare how customers respond to two different pricing options. Customers are randomly assigned to the control group (A) or test group (B) and shown different pricing variations, and their responses are compared. A/B price testing can help you make data-driven pricing decisions based on actual customer behavior.


### Is A/B price testing effective?


A/B price testing can be effective when you have a clear hypothesis and enough traffic and sales to generate meaningful results. Make sure your test product has ample inventory, and account for seasonal demand, promotions, and other factors that could affect customer behavior.


### How do you test whether you’re setting the right price?


To test a product’s price, split your customers into two groups and present each group with a different pricing page. After you run your test, analyze the buying behavior of each group using metrics such as conversion rate, revenue, or AOV to determine how the pricing change affected your business performance.
